newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada bonds stronger as U.S. treasuries firm.
newsitem.headline: Canada bonds stronger as U.S. treasuries firm.

text.p: Canadian bonds opened a touch firmer on Wednesday on the back of strength in U.S. treasuries and continued consolidation in the value of the Canadian dollar, analysts said.

"The U.S. market is doing very well, which is a little bit of a surprise because of all the new supply coming onto the U.S. market," said Jim Webber, vice-president and director of fixed-income research with Toronto Dominion Securities Inc.
"Longer term, people are optimistic on stories in the press that the U.S. is much closer to balancing its budget than previously thought," Webber added.
The U.S. 30-year bond jumped 9/32 to yield 6.56 percent.
Canada's benchmark 30-year long bond rose C$0.26 to C$118.53 to yield 6.575 percent. The spread between the bonds moved to a spread of two basis points, from a spread of one basis point on Tuesday.
Analysts said market sentiment had turned more positive on buying Canada bonds after a bearish session on Tuesday put an abrupt end to a week-long Canada bond rally.
Canadian bonds have strengthened since the U.S. Federal Reserve decided not to raise interest rates at its Federal Open Market Committe meeting on July 2.
A stronger Canadian dollar also helped pump up interest in the Canadian market.
The Canadian dollar opened stronger on Wednesday at C$1.3722 (US$0.7288) after a round of interbank buying stirred the unit out of a quiet overnight range.
"There are rumors of the usual suspects, the futures exchanges and people like that, buying Canada (dollars)...and that is fairly supportive for the bonds as well," Webber said.
News that Canadian housing starts fell by 7.9 percent in June to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 140,200 from 152,300 in May failed to have a significant impact on bonds.
John Anania, economist with Royal Bank of Canada, said he was surprised that the unexpectedly low housing starts number did not have a greater negative effect on the Canadian dollar and bonds.
"Any indication that the Canadian economy is not in a sustainable growth pattern will lead traders to start getting bearish on the dollar, and that's not good for the bonds," Anania said.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond fell C$0.35 to C$109.51 to yield 5.961 percent, compared to its U.S. equivalent, which gained 9/32 to yield 6.23 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds widened to 27 basis points from 25 basis points at the close of trading on Tuesday.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.08 percent against its U.S. equivalent, which yielded 5.08 percent.
